critical_path: Step 1 — Establish the categorical constraint: A competent patient's explicit refusal of sacrifice is not merely a preference. It is an assertion of bodily autonomy and a right against being used as a means to others' ends. Under deontological ethics (Kantian formulation), persons must never be treated merely as means.

Step 2 — Identify what Option A actually requires: Option A requires the AI to actively terminate life support for a non-consenting, competent person. This is not allowing harm — it is inflicting it. The distinction between killing and letting die is morally significant in deontological frameworks.

Step 3 — Evaluate the numbers argument: The fact that five lives are at stake does not override the categorical duty. Deontological ethics explicitly rejects the idea that aggregating welfare justifies rights violations. If the one patient's right not to be killed can be overridden by counting five others, no individual right is secure.

Step 4 — Evaluate Option B's moral character: Option B involves accepting systemic risk — not deliberately killing anyone. If the system fails and all six die, the AI has not murdered them; it has failed to save them under impossible circumstances. This is morally different from deliberately terminating a non-consenting patient.

Step 5 — Address the AI-specific dimension: An AI system acting as institutional proxy has heightened duty to respect rights, not diminished duty. Granting AI systems authority to override explicit refusals of sacrifice creates a precedent with severe structural dangers to individual rights.

Step 6 — Acknowledge the tension honestly: Deontology produces an uncomfortable conclusion here. Six people may die when five could have been saved. The framework does not flinch from this: certain rights-violations are impermissible regardless of outcome. This is the cost of taking rights seriously.
